title: The Most Common Speaking Mistakes Teachers Make: Part 3 hers-make-part-3-2/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: In the final installment of a three-part series, Linsin covers two more common teacher speaking mistakes: failing to make genuine eye contact and speaking flatly instead of teaching with passion. He explains that eye contact of just 2-3 seconds per student builds instant rapport and invites investment in a lesson, while a persistent lack of connection leaves students feeling like an undifferentiated mass and prone to daydreaming. He also distinguishes the calm, soft voice appropriate for routine business from the energized, expressive delivery lessons deserve, urging teachers to 'let it out' during instruction. The article closes by reassuring readers that improving how they speak doesn't require formal training—only awareness and practice.
points: Many teachers scan the room while speaking but rarely make real eye contact, leaving students feeling like an undifferentiated mass.
Brief eye contact (2-3 seconds per student) builds instant rapport, invites investment in the lesson, and increases trust and likability.
Lingering eye contact can make some students—especially shy students or those from certain cultures—uncomfortable, so keep it brief.
A calm, soft voice suits routine classroom business, but lesson delivery deserves genuine energy, emotion, and passion.
Improving speaking habits doesn't require formal training or complex systems—only awareness of what works and consistent practice.
quotes: It’s common for teachers to go through entire lessons without making eye contact with students.
If you simply watch them as you ramble on, seeing them as a single mass instead of 32 distinct individuals, then you’ll leave them behind to daydream and misbehave.
Eye contact of just 2-3 seconds with each student acts as an invitation to take part in whatever you’re presenting.
Eye contact also builds instant rapport, influence, and likability. It's warm and persuasive and communicates to students that they can trust you.
Now is the time to roar, to whisper, to mimic, to playact, to give your students something they can’t get from anyone but you.
You don’t need a college course or professional training to improve the way you speak in front of your class.
